comments.text:
again, there is a huge difference between alphafold and q* as described here. Alphafold did not 'solve' protein folding. It does not come up with a discrete solution, but an analog one, one that could work just as well as any other one. Just like alphazero. It did not 'solve' go. It came up with an approximation of the perfect solution, not the perfect solution itself.

But here they are expecting us to believe that q* is so good that it basically cracked P=NP and gave us an exact solution to a discrete problem in mathematics by tunneling to THE global minima in a series of math landscapes (that's what a proof is, solving a global minima problem across a sea of symbols) and then applying that global minima to an.encrypted piece of text, just by looking at it? Just plain ridiculous, bordering on comical. You don't get any points for being close in a decryption of a text. Think of a sudoku. You get to the end, and you see that one digit just doesn't fit. It is - most of the time - inordinately difficult to backtrack to find the point of the error, most of the time you just need to go back to the beginning and solve again.

And just think of how much more difficult an AES-192 cipher is. If you don't have the exact key, you have no idea of how close the actual key would be. There is no 'search landscape' analogous to protein folding or to Go.

This is so obviously BS that i'm despairing at how gullible people that I thought - who I know - are more intelligent than this are falling for it. I don't know, maybe its just because people like believing in a conspiracy but I'm really despairing here. It seems that we are really ossifying fast as a society here, and the LAST thing we need here is to bow to conspiracies.

I think I can see how an AI model can break any public key encryption scheme... and it's so simple (and in line with what AI LLM models do) that's it's kind of baffling how no one came up with it before... well, kind of baffling, but not really, as humans don't think like AIs process data, so it's really not that surprising that no mathematician has come up with it before.

It all starts with this simple fact: Encryption is a function that maps a set of values into another set of values.

This may seem obvious at first, but let me expand on that that a little.

Imagine encryption scheme that works on a set of (all possible) plain texts (unencrypted messages), where each message can be up to a certain number of bits long. Let's denote the number of (unencrypted) message bits as N. Let's also denote the number of bits of encrypted message as M, and the number of bits of keys as Ke. Note that, in general, N and M don't have to be the same, and is even possible to have M < N, which is commonly known as compression (which is really a form of encryption, where algorithm acts as [the only] "encryption key").

Now, we can define a set of functions that are encrypting our messages, and denote it as F.

In other words, we will use as many functions f[i] as there are (M) bits in the encrypted message, where each function f[i] will take as its inputs all the (N) bits of the original (unencrypted) message, and produce a single bit of the encrypted message, where i denotes the position of that bit in the encrypted message (that is, 0 <= i < M).

Our set of function F now defines the *composite encryption function*.

Now, let's do the same thing, but in reverse , and define a set of decryption functions. Let's denote that set as G, and each function in the set as g[j], where 0 <= j < N (because we are now "encrypting" the already encrypted message that's M bits long, which will now give us the N bits of the original, unencrypted message). Let's denote decryption key as Kd.

Let us now analyze all of the above, and look at some possibilities:
* M = N, Ke = Kd (G = F) : classical, symmetrical encryption scheme
* M = N, Ke =/= Kd (G =/= F)  : classical, asymmetrical public-key encryption scheme
* M < N, Ke = Kd (where Ke and Kd are hard-encoded within the algorithm itself, and thus, G = F) : compression scheme
* M > N, Ke ? Kd (either case) : an encryption scheme that I have never seen being defined anywhere, but obviously an encryption scheme, nonetheless

So, the question now arises: How can an AI model use all of this to crack any public-key encryption scheme, regardless of the key length ?

And the answer to that question lies in the method we have used to define function sets F and G... specifically, the G one.

In other words, one can go about it by training the model to build the set G, with large enough training sets of both unencrypted and (their corresponding) encrypted texts.

Do you see where this is all going?

If you don't, then let me put it all in plan text (pun intended): By building the set G, we have effectively created a composite decryption function that works for all possible encrypted messages , and thus we (out AI model) can now decrypt every single public-key "encrypted" message, and -- to add insult to the injury(!) -- we can decrypt any message without even knowing the encryption key that was used for that particular message!

Man...

Is public-key "encryption" a -- both horrifying and [Monty] Pythonesque-deadly -- joke or what?!
